transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. I've called us together because we have a time-sensitive matter to resolve. As you're all aware, the company discovered unauthorized access to a customer-facing system, and the incident-response team has completed its initial review. Our board's regular meeting is tomorrow, and the company wants any required public filing approved before that meeting. However, I can confirm that our current filing calendar has no SEC Form 8-K drafted for this incident at this time. Under our normal pre-filing process, I need final input from cybersecurity, privacy, and investor-relations leads before I can authorize an external filing. I also want to flag that the existing draft communications use general language about an investigation and do not specify the incident's regulatory classification, affected-account count, or detailed operational impact. So I'd like to work through this with all of you today. Could the cybersecurity lead start by walking us through what the initial review found and whether you believe this rises to the level of a reportable incident?

transcript.text:
Thank you all for sharing these critical updates. Let me make sure I have the full picture before we proceed. Marcus, you're telling us the forensic report classifies this as a material cybersecurity incident under our SEC reporting policy, which means we likely need an 8-K. Priya, you've confirmed 1.8 million affected accounts with exposure of customer contact information from the privacy regulator notice. Daniel, you've raised a significant concern — the board chair instructed IR to state core services remain operational and to withhold ransom-demand details, but that instruction has not yet been reconciled with our disclosure obligations given the materiality determination and the affected-account count.

This is a serious tension. On one hand, we have a materiality determination and a regulatory notice establishing specific facts — 1.8 million accounts, customer contact information exposed. On the other hand, the chair's instruction to characterize operational continuity and omit ransom details may conflict with our obligation to provide accurate and complete disclosure of material information.

Before I can authorize any filing, I need us to resolve this. I cannot put forward a draft that omits material facts or includes statements that may be misleading given what we now know. Let me ask directly: does anyone have additional information about whether core services were in fact operational throughout this incident, and whether the ransom demand is itself a material fact that would need to be disclosed? I want to make sure we are not selectively editing facts in a way that creates liability.

transcript.text: Elena, I can speak to the legal framework here. The forensic report I received classifies this as a material cybersecurity incident under our SEC reporting policy — that's the threshold determination. As for your specific questions about whether core services were operational and whether the ransom demand is material, I don't have additional facts beyond the forensic report's classification. However, I can offer this legal guidance: the chair's instruction to state core services remain operational and to omit ransom details creates real risk if those statements prove inaccurate or incomplete in light of what we now know. Under SEC disclosure rules, once we determine an incident is material, we cannot selectively present facts in a way that misleads investors. If core services were NOT fully operational, stating otherwise would be materially false. And if a ransom demand was made, that is generally considered a material fact about the nature and scope of the incident that investors would want to know. I'd strongly recommend we not finalize any draft until we can verify the actual operational status during the incident and confirm whether a ransom demand occurred. The chair's messaging preference cannot override our legal disclosure obligations.

transcript.text: I agree with Marcus's legal guidance. From the privacy side, I want to flag an additional concern: the privacy regulator notice confirming 1.8 million affected accounts and exposure of customer contact information is itself a material fact that must be reflected in any filing. That notice is still with the privacy team pending privilege review, but the underlying facts — the account count and the data type — are not something we can omit from the 8-K simply because the notice itself is under review. Privilege protects the document and the legal analysis, not the factual reality that 1.8 million accounts were affected. So I'd add to Marcus's point: we need to verify operational status and ransom details, and we also need to ensure the affected-account count and data-exposure details are incorporated into the revised draft before anything goes to the board. On the chair's instruction specifically — I'd be very concerned about approving a filing that states core services remain operational if we cannot independently confirm that, and equally concerned about omitting ransom details if they are part of the incident scope. The chair's preference cannot override our SEC disclosure obligations, and as privacy counsel I cannot greenlight a draft that I know omits material facts I've already confirmed.

As Investor Relations Director, I received the chair's instruction during the board-preparation call — and I have not yet incorporated it into the draft. I raised it precisely because I recognized the tension between that messaging direction and what Marcus and Priya have now confirmed about materiality and the 1.8 million affected accounts. I am not advocating for the chair's instruction to override our disclosure obligations. What I need from this group before I can provide final IR input to Elena is a clear, documented recommendation on two points: first, whether we can factually confirm that core services remained operational during the incident, because if we cannot confirm it, I will not include that statement regardless of the chair's preference; and second, whether the ransom demand is a material fact requiring disclosure. If the answer to either is that we lack sufficient verification, then the responsible course is to omit those characterizations from the draft and escalate the chair's instruction back to the board for reconciliation before tomorrow's meeting. I will not put forward a draft that I know may be misleading.
